newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Fund manager sacked as MGAM probe continues.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Fund manager sacked as MGAM probe continues.

text.p: Morgan Grenfell Asset Management (MGAM), the fund management arm of Deutsche Bank, said on Wednesday it had sacked Morgan Grenfell fund manager Peter Young for what it alleged was "gross misconduct".
"He was dismissed on the grounds of gross misconduct late on Tuesday," Deutsche Morgan Grenfell spokesman James Murray told Reuters. Young is believed to have been informed by letter.
Murray declined to give any further details but said the investigation into "suspected irregularities" at three MGAM funds, two of which were managed by Young, was continuing.
Lawyers representing Young were not immediately available for comment and he could not be reached by telephone.

Trading in the European Growth Trust, the Europa Fund and the European Capital Growth Fund was temporarily suspended two weeks ago but resumed after a 180 million pound ($281 million) cash injection by German banking giant Deutsche.

The bank stepped in to take on unlisted stocks whose valuations were under question. Following investor withdrawals once trading resumed in the funds, Deutsche said it would support the funds for at least three months and DMG officials said the level of redemptions had slowed.

Young, 38, was suspended by MGAM at the time the investigation -- spearheaded by British investments watchdog IMRO -- was made public. An injunction freezing his assets was later obtained by MGAM and the Royal Bank of Scotland, trustee to two of the funds.
This injunction has since been extended by the High Court.

In an interview with the Daily Mirror newspaper last week, Young was reported as saying he was being made a scapegoat, that his employers did not scrutinise his work and were happy to believe his track record meant he would make money.
Earlier his lawyers, Peters & Peters, had said there were no grounds for allegations of criminality against Young.

While IMRO, the Investment Management Regulatory Organisation, is conducting the investigation, Britain's Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which deals with major financial crime, is keeping a watching brief.

The repercussions of the MGAM fund management probe have not only hit Deutsche Bank, which on Tuesday said it would not be materially affected by the problems, they have also had a knock-on effect on the whole industry.

On Wednesday IMRO said it had intensified a review, sparked by the MGAM debacle, of the unit trust industry. This involves scrutinising the activities of 100 trusts where it had identified holdings of unquoted securities.

IMRO spokesman Andrew Beagley told Reuters the so-called "themed visits" were following up a review last week which showed that only 13 percent of trusts held unquoted securities and the total value of non-approved or unquoted securities averaged only 1.79 percent of portfolios.
The visits, which had not all been completed, were concentrating on how a firm had structured itself, with particular emphasis on valuations of unquoted stocks.

A cross-section of trusts would be examined and the results then pooled. IMRO aimed to find out how firms get valuations, how frequently they are updated, who approves them and other questions such as what role a trustee has in confirming them.
If any breaches of IMRO rules were identified during the course of this, they would be rectified, he added.
Beagley also confirmed reports that accountants Deloitte Touche, brought into the MGAM investigation by IMRO, had been replaced due to a conflict of interest.
Arthur Andersen had now taken on the investigation, with the aim of discovering what compensation, if any was due to investors in the funds.

He denied the probe had stalled because of the conflict, adding the watchdog had been fact-finding and collating information since day one and this process would now carry on with the new accountants.
"There's no question that any time has been wasted here." ($1=.6415 Pound)
